I disagree that it is impossible to test. They could perfectly well build a test lab that could validate frequent updates. They have just chosen not to.

Microsoft used to be legendary for testing the crap out of new versions. Backwards compatibility was king. Somewhere they have lost the way.

I've been developing software (mostly embedded stuff) for 25 years.

It is absolutely impossible to fully test an entire operating system of the scope of Windows (or Linux for that matter) in a week or a month. And yes, even if you update only one tool or library, a system test by definition requires a test of the ENTIRE SYSTEM for unintended or unforeseen consequences of the upgrade. By releasing updates so frequently M$ is only testing the smallest fraction of what should be tested, assuming they're doing anything beyond simple unit tests at this point.

Microsoft has the budget to automate most of the release tests. If they wanted to they could make an automated test lab with thousands of different machines and peripherals, with simulated hard drives and I/O subsystems to drive them. It would cost a few hundred million dollars, but they could do it. They used to nearly do this using manual testing and code reviews, so it is not impossible. For several decades they were the pinnacle of backwards compatibility.

Recently they are just crapping out release after release with cursory testing. Hopefully they will have a mountain-visits-Mohammed moment before they go bankrupt. They did this before when the Internet ate their lunch, and again when security problems threatened to destroy their value proposition. But back then they had Bill Gates to kick them into shape. Will they be able to remake the company again?

Google does exactly this today. They have vast regression testing infrastructure that they run on every single source code delta. They test every requirement that has ever been noticed, and make sure every bug fix still works. Massive regression testing is possible. If you have the will.

I feel like it's not cost efficient to test everything THAT thoroughly. As said Windows user base isn't going anywhere. Roll it out, see what happens, patch accordingly. I might be wrong with economies of scale and Windows being fucking huge. We can all agree on which is the lazier, easy route though.
